strengths: The paper addresses the timely and important problem of cross-generator AI-image detection and identifies spatial shortcut learning as a potentially useful perspective.
PPL is simple and practically compatible with pretrained ViTs: random patch replacement and patch-level contrastive learning are intuitive complementary components.
The experiments cover three datasets, two training/testing settings, two backbones, corruption and masking tests, and a component ablation. The reported GenImage and DRCT results are strong.
The manuscript is generally understandable and uses useful qualitative visualizations to communicate the intended behavior.
weaknesses: The central claim that all patches contain useful, uniformly distributed artifacts is not established. Being generated does not imply that every local crop has detectable forensic evidence. The cited 90% result averages over randomly selected patches on one seen SDv1.4 subset, while a few visual examples cannot prove the universal claim or its cross-generator validity.

The purported causal analysis is technically unjustified. The defined TDE is ordinary zero-occlusion logit sensitivity, not an identified causal direct effect; zero masking is an out-of-distribution intervention and can change predictions for reasons unrelated to synthetic evidence. The paper provides neither causal assumptions nor aggregate statistics linking TDE uniformity to generalization, and the claimed lazy-learner root cause remains speculative.

Critical methodological details are missing, including patch size/count, replacement rate, contrastive margin and weight, token/layer selection, sampling and normalization, patch labels after replacement, the image-level label for mixed images, reconstruction procedure, and most optimization settings. The promised appendix is absent, substantially limiting reproducibility and even leaving the training objective ambiguous.

The comparisons are insufficiently controlled. The proposed models use large CLIP/DINOv2 backbones, LoRA, and additional diffusion-reconstructed paired images, whereas most baseline numbers are copied from other papers with potentially different backbones, data, augmentations, and training budgets. Same-backbone and same-data reimplementations are needed to isolate PPL.

Aligned real/fake patch replacement may introduce seams or reconstruction-specific cues. There are no controls using CutMix, random erasing, patch dropout, unaligned replacements, boundary smoothing, global supervised contrastive learning, or equal amounts of reconstructed training data, so the gains do not specifically validate the proposed patch-coverage mechanism. The overall novelty relative to standard patch mixing and supervised contrastive learning is therefore limited.

There are concrete reporting problems. In Table 2, both proposed rows report std = 0.1, although the displayed per-domain values imply standard deviations of approximately 1.24 and 0.45. No results across random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are given.

The strongest real-world-style result is overstated: on Chameleon with all GenImage training, DINOv2 detects only 49.68% of fake images while obtaining 88.99% real-image accuracy. Reporting only aggregate accuracy on this imbalanced test set obscures this failure mode; balanced accuracy, AUROC, calibration, and threshold analysis are needed.

Robustness evidence is narrow: corruption tests use the seen SDv1.4 domain, masking resembles the training intervention, and no uncertainty is shown. The method is also restricted to fully generated images and does not evaluate localized edits or mixed real/synthetic content, despite these being important deployment cases.

Likewise, no controlled experiment directly demonstrates monotonically improving generalization as more distinct patches are used. The visual examples and attention maps are anecdotal.

The quantity called a Controlled Direct Effect is only zero-mask occlusion sensitivity. No causal graph, identification assumptions, or treatment/outcome model is supplied; zero masking also creates out-of-distribution inputs. Patch interactions, model confidence, and logit calibration can all change this score. Per-image normalization and selected heatmaps cannot establish that uniform causal contribution produces generalization, and no quantitative uniformity metric or correlation across detectors is reported.

The headline comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Many results are imported from papers using different architectures, training data, preprocessing, and optimization, while the proposed method uses large pretrained backbones plus additional diffusion-reconstructed data. The cross-dataset tables explicitly compare different training distributions. A same-backbone, same-data, same-budget comparison against naive LoRA, DRCT, patch mixing/dropout, and other strongest baselines is needed.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on accuracy without repeated-run uncertainty, AUROC, AP, F1, or calibration analysis. This is particularly problematic for the imbalanced Chameleon benchmark: the best all-GenImage model obtains 72.07% overall accuracy while detecting only 49.68% of fake images, which does not support the claimed strong real-world generalization. The validation protocol is absent, so the extensive hyperparameter selection may have used the reported test generators.

Reproducibility is poor: optimizer, learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, LoRA rank and target layers, sampling details for contrastive pairs, data counts and splits, decision thresholds, random seeds, and code availability are missing. The stated all-pairs margin loss remains quadratic, contrary to the appendix's efficiency rationale, unless an unreported sampling scheme is used.

There are material internal inconsistencies. The text alternates between replacing real patches with reconstructed patches and replacing reconstructed patches with real ones; the patch-label construction is underspecified; and using a zero-filled inpainting mask is ambiguous. In Table 2, the displayed domain values imply standard deviations of roughly 1.3 and 0.5 for the two proposed models, not 0.1; if 0.1 instead denotes run variation, it is incomparable to baseline columns. Table 8 also shows the best result at patch size 28 rather than the claimed preference for the smallest size.

Novelty is limited relative to diffusion reconstruction, patch mixing/dropout, patch-level supervision, and supervised contrastive learning, while the distinction from DRCT and Breaking is not isolated experimentally. The paper also omits a substantive limitations and ethics discussion, including false-positive harms and the explicit restriction to fully generated rather than partially edited images.

strengths: The paper addresses the timely and important problem of detecting AI-generated images and identifies regional shortcut reliance as an intuitively plausible failure mode.

PPL is conceptually simple and potentially useful: randomized patch reconstruction supplies localized supervision, while patch-wise contrastive learning encourages separable patch representations across both CLIP and DINOv2 backbones.

The empirical scope is broad, covering several cross-generator and cross-dataset benchmarks, an in-the-wild dataset, common corruptions, and two backbone families. The reported gains on GenImage and DRCT-2M are substantial.
The paper includes useful ablations over individual components, reconstruction ratio and location, patch size, contrastive loss, and patch dropout, together with CDE and Grad-CAM visualizations.
weaknesses: The central principles are not convincingly established. A hand-picked reconstruction example and a briefly described single-patch experiment on only SDv1.4 do not show that every patch contains detectable artifacts across generators. Likewise, the association between broader heatmaps and accuracy does not demonstrate that using more patches causes better generalization. The full-generation assumption also excludes composites and localized edits encountered in practice.

The paper mischaracterizes an occlusion-based logit difference as a Controlled Direct Effect. Zeroing a patch is an out-of-distribution perturbation, and no causal model or identification assumptions are provided. Uniform occlusion sensitivity need not mean that the model uses every patch productively, and the claimed connection between CDE uniformity and generalization is largely qualitative.

RPR introduces a serious augmentation confound: mosaicking original and diffusion-reconstructed pixels on a fixed patch grid can create boundary, VAE, or inpainting artifacts that are easier to learn than authentic generation traces. Controls using seamless blending, randomized grid offsets, alternative reconstruction models, and fully reconstructed images are missing. Descriptions also alternate between replacing real patches with reconstructed ones and replacing fake patches with real ones, making the exact procedure unclear.

The main comparisons are insufficiently controlled. The proposed models use strong CLIP-Large/DINOv2 backbones, whereas many baselines are copied from prior papers, use different architectures or preprocessing, and—on some benchmarks—are trained on different datasets. A matched plain-LoRA baseline is shown only in a limited ablation figure. The exceptionally large DRCT-2M results particularly require controls for dataset-construction artifacts or leakage.

There are no repeated-run results, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the reported standard deviations are across generator subsets rather than training runs. Accuracy alone is inadequate for this detection setting. On Chameleon, the best reported overall accuracy masks weak fake-image accuracy—49.68% for DINOv2 and 38.93% for CLIP under AllGenImage training—so the claim of strong real-world generalization is overstated. The validation protocol for hyperparameter selection is also unspecified.

Reproducibility and technical specification are inadequate: optimizer, learning rate, batch size, LoRA rank and target layers, exact backbone variants, training schedule, seeds, and pair-sampling details are absent, with no code link. Algorithm 1 combines two logits of shape [B,2] with BCE labels of shape [B], which is dimensionally inconsistent, and the appendix incorrectly suggests the margin loss avoids computing all negative-pair distances despite its all-pairs formulation.

The methodological novelty is modest relative to existing patch augmentation and supervised contrastive approaches, while the paper provides no limitations or risk analysis concerning false accusations from detector errors. Given the unsupported central interpretation and confounded evaluation, the evidence is not yet competitive for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

Panoptic Patch Learning is intuitive: randomized partial reconstruction diversifies positive cues, while patch-level contrastive learning encourages locally discriminative representations. Results with both CLIP and DINOv2 suggest some backbone portability.

The empirical scope is broad, covering GenImage, DRCT-2M, AIGCDetectionBenchmark, UniversalFakeDetect, Chameleon, multiple generator families, and several image corruptions. Many reported improvements are substantial.

The paper includes useful component and hyperparameter studies, comparisons of contrastive losses, fixed versus random reconstruction, patch sizes, and patch dropout, plus extensive attribution visualizations.
weaknesses: The central claim that every patch contains synthetic artifacts is much stronger than the evidence. Selected visual examples and 90% accuracy after replicating one patch do not establish universality; replication itself creates unnatural tiling and distribution shifts. The paper also does not systematically test every position across generators and image contents.

The purported Controlled Direct Effect is actually zero-mask occlusion sensitivity, without a causal model or controlled mediators. Zeroing creates an out-of-distribution black patch, so the resulting logit change can reflect masking artifacts or contextual disruption. More uniform occlusion maps correlating with accuracy does not demonstrate that broader patch use causes generalization.

Several comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Results are imported from different papers, use different backbones and preprocessing, and, in Tables 3–4, compare systems trained on different source distributions. Same-backbone, same-data reimplementations are needed to support the state-of-the-art and mechanism claims.

An important alternative explanation remains untested: RPR may teach the detector reconstruction-model fingerprints, hard patch-boundary seams, or grid-aligned artifacts rather than broadly distributed generative cues. Controls such as real-to-real reconstruction, seamless blending, shifted or irregular grids, multiple reconstruction models, and standard CutMix/GridMask augmentations are missing.

The novelty is moderate relative to DRCT-style reconstruction, patch mixing or dropout, and supervised contrastive learning. The paper does not adequately compare against straightforward combinations of these existing techniques or a direct patch-level classification objective.

Some reported analyses are internally unclear. Figure 8 has different +LoRA baselines before the nominal RPR/PCL comparison, confounding the component attribution. In Table 2, the listed DINOv2 and CLIP accuracies have across-column standard deviations of roughly 1.28 and 0.47, respectively, rather than the reported 0.1; the meaning of the uncertainty terms is not defined.

Reproducibility is inadequate: exact backbone variants, optimizer, learning rate, LoRA rank and target layers, batch size, epoch count, seeds, repeated-run variability, threshold selection, and complete data splits are absent. The zero-filled inpainting mask is ambiguous under standard mask conventions, and the pseudocode applies BCE to two logits with scalar labels.

The real-world conclusion is overstated. On Chameleon, the best 72.07% overall result corresponds to 49.68% fake-image accuracy versus 88.99% real-image accuracy, indicating substantial class bias. The paper provides no calibration, AUC/AP, confidence intervals, or deployment analysis, and it omits limitations and ethical discussion concerning false accusations and domain-dependent failures.
